The enrichment analysis has identified **Arachidonic Acid Metabolism** as the dominant affected pathway, with all six of the tested metabolites confirmed members of this network. CDP is the sole outlier, consistent with its distinct biochemical role. The KEGG Arachidonic Acid Metabolism pathway (map00590) and its associated SMPDB drug-action pathways all achieve FDR = 0.0 with massive fold-enrichment (≥723), driven by six matched metabolites: arachidonic acid, leukotriene A4, 5-HETE, 15-HETE, 15-deoxy-Δ12,14-PGJ2, and 11,12,15-THETA.

**Pathway interpretation and key drivers**

Arachidonic acid (C00219) is the upstream substrate that feeds three downstream metabolic branches. The KEGG reaction graph confirms that arachidonic acid is connected to leukotriene A4 (C00909) in just two enzymatic steps via an epoxy intermediate, establishing arachidonic acid as the upstream driver of the leukotriene arm. Leukotriene A4 itself is the unstable epoxide precursor to the cysteinyl-leukotriene series (LTC4, LTD4, LTE4) and is a well-established mediator of inflammation and bronchoconstriction.

The simultaneous elevation of 5-HETE and 15-HETE alongside leukotriene A4 is consistent with enhanced 5-lipoxygenase and 15-lipoxygenase activity acting on arachidonic acid. 15-Deoxy-Δ12,14-PGJ2 (a cyclopentenone prostaglandin) and 11,12,15-THETA (a trihydroxy-eicosatrienoic acid) point to parallel cyclooxygenase and cytochrome-P450 epoxygenase分流. Importantly, 15-Deoxy-d-12,14-PGJ2 has no downstream neighbours in the reaction network — it is a terminal bioactive metabolite — which makes its accumulation a direct readout of pathway activation rather than further conversion.

**Biological significance**

Coordinated up-regulation of lipoxygenase and cycloxygenase products from a common arachidonic acid pool is a hallmark of active inflammation, tissue injury, or oxidative stress. Leukotriene A4 and its downstream leukotrienes are strongly implicated in asthma, inflammatory bowel disease, and cardiovascular inflammation, whereas 15-Deoxy-Δ12,14-PGJ2 acts as both a pro-inflammatory mediator and a PPAR-γ agonist with context-dependent anti-inflammatory effects. The presence of CDP (cytidine diphosphate) in the dataset may reflect broader phospholipid remodelling or nucleotide Second Messenger perturbations that often accompany inflammatory activation. The enrichment of drug-action pathways (NSAID/acetaminophen/rofecoxib) in the background further underscores that the observed eicosanoid fingerprint is pharmacologically and physiologically meaningful.
